title: Exclusivity in Accord 1 covers only established protocols, leaving new deployments to a right of first refusal
content:
A.2.8.2.1.2.2 gives Grove exclusivity over Real World Assets, carved back so it "does not extend to Treasuries used for ASC purposes or stablecoin liquidity provisioning." A.2.8.2.1.2.3 gives Spark exclusivity over "Maple, cryptocurrency OTC lending, and Established DeFi Lending Protocols," and A.2.8.2.1.2.3.1 defines those as "DeFi lending protocols deployed six months ago or earlier."

The six-month test does more work than it appears to. By restricting exclusivity to mature protocols it deliberately leaves *new* protocols outside anyone's exclusive domain — and A.2.8.2.1.2.4 catches them with a different instrument, Grove granting Spark "a right of first refusal for DeFi opportunities on unclaimed chains and new protocols."

So the Accord allocates opportunity two ways depending on maturity. Established territory is divided by hard boundaries, which is efficient when the landscape is known and the value is in avoiding duplicated effort. Frontier territory is allocated by a timed option, which is appropriate when nobody can enumerate in advance what will appear.

Grove's carve-outs point the same way: Treasuries for Actively Stabilizing Collateral and stablecoin liquidity are excluded from RWA exclusivity because both are *requirements* every Prime must satisfy, not opportunities to be claimed. A.2.8.2.1.2.6 confirms it from the other side, preserving Spark's right to deploy into tokenized US Treasury Bills for ASC.

The pattern worth extracting: exclusivity should attach to what is knowable, and compliance obligations should never be exclusive to one party — otherwise the other cannot meet its own requirements.
description: Spark's exclusivity extends to DeFi lending protocols deployed six months ago or earlier, so anything newer is allocated by ROFR instead
